questions.stem: A manager describes incident handling as 'the containment step we run when an alert fires.' What is wrong with that description?

options.text: Incident handling is the whole lifecycle: preparing, detecting, responding, and learning, repeated over time
options.rationale: Correct: it is the umbrella process, not one step.

options.text: Incident handling covers only the post-incident meeting
options.rationale: The meeting is one part of a much larger process.

options.text: Incident handling is a one-time project that ends when the plan is written
options.rationale: It runs continuously as a lifecycle.

options.text: Nothing; incident handling and containment are the same thing
options.rationale: Containment is one phase within incident handling.

questions.explanation: Incident handling is the overall process of preparing for, detecting, responding to, and learning from incidents. It runs as a lifecycle rather than a one-time event, and containment is only one phase inside it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Incident handling is the full lifecycle, not one phase or one-time event.

questions.stem: Which of these is a security incident rather than just an event?

options.text: An attacker's script encrypts files on a file server, making them unavailable
options.rationale: Correct: an event with an adverse effect on availability.

options.text: A user signs in successfully at 9 a.m.
options.rationale: An ordinary observable occurrence, so an event.

options.text: A server writes a routine backup-completed message to its log
options.rationale: An event with no adverse effect.

options.text: A firewall logs a permitted connection to the company website
options.rationale: Normal traffic, so an event.

questions.explanation: An event is any observable occurrence in a system or network. A security incident is an event that violates or threatens security policy or harms confidentiality, integrity, or availability.
questions.discriminator_tested: Event = any observable occurrence; incident = an event with an adverse effect.

questions.stem: A ransomware incident is under way: one workstation's files are being encrypted and a ransom note has appeared. What should the responders do first?

options.text: Isolate the workstation from the network to contain the spread
options.rationale: Correct: containment comes first.

options.text: Pay the ransom immediately to get the decryption key
options.rationale: Payment follows a policy set in advance, and paying neither stops the spread nor guarantees recovery.

options.text: Restore the workstation from backup while it is still connected
options.rationale: Restoring before containing and removing the ransomware risks the restored files being encrypted again.

options.text: Email the ransom note to all staff so they recognize it
options.rationale: That informs people but does nothing to stop the spread.

questions.explanation: In a ransomware incident, data is encrypted for payment. Response relies on isolation, clean backups, and a payment policy decided in advance: contain first, then restore from clean backups.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ransomware: contain first, restore from clean backups later.

questions.stem: A caller posing as an executive talked the help desk into resetting the executive's password and reading the new one back. The caller then had access to the executive's email for a day. Which response to this social engineering incident fits best?

options.text: Reset the executive's credentials, review what the account accessed, and retrain help desk staff on identity verification
options.rationale: Correct: credential reset plus education.

options.text: Replace the email server hardware
options.rationale: The server wasn't the weakness; people were manipulated.

options.text: Permanently disable the executive's account
options.rationale: The executive is the victim; resetting and reviewing is enough.

options.text: Take no action, since no malware was involved
options.rationale: Unauthorized access to email is still an incident.

questions.explanation: A social engineering incident manipulates people into giving access or information. Response includes credential resets, checking what was accessed, and user education so the same trick fails next time.
questions.discriminator_tested: Social engineering response: credential resets plus user education.

questions.stem: Several staff received a phishing email linking to a fake sign-in page, and two of them entered their passwords. Which two actions belong in the response to this phishing incident? (Choose two.)

options.text: Block the sender and the malicious URL
options.rationale: Correct: stops more people reaching the page.

options.text: Reset the passwords of the two users who entered them
options.rationale: Correct: those credentials are exposed.

options.text: Reply to the sender asking them to stop
options.rationale: Engaging the attacker helps nothing and confirms the address is monitored.

options.text: Delete the reported email without recording anything
options.rationale: It should be reported and kept, not silently destroyed.

options.text: Reinstall the operating system on every company workstation
options.rationale: Disproportionate; the exposure was credentials.

questions.explanation: A phishing incident uses fraudulent messages to steal credentials or deliver malware. Respond by reporting it, blocking the sender and URLs, and resetting any exposed credentials.
questions.discriminator_tested: Phishing: report, block sender and URLs, reset exposed credentials.

questions.stem: A DDoS incident is saturating the company's internet link with traffic from thousands of addresses. Blocking at the company's own firewall doesn't help, because the link itself is full. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Ask the ISP to filter the traffic upstream, before it reaches the link
options.rationale: Correct: only filtering upstream relieves a full link.

options.text: Block the single attacking IP address
options.rationale: There are thousands of sources, not one.

options.text: Restart the firewall
options.rationale: Restarting doesn't reduce the incoming volume.

options.text: Reimage the web server
options.rationale: The server isn't compromised; the link is flooded.

questions.explanation: A DDoS incident floods a resource with traffic from many sources. When the flood fills the link before local filters ever see it, mitigation needs upstream help from the ISP.
questions.discriminator_tested: DDoS mitigation often needs upstream ISP filtering.

questions.stem: Hundreds of companies discover that a properly signed update from a trusted network-management vendor contained a backdoor. What kind of attack is this?

options.text: A supply chain attack
options.rationale: Correct: the compromise came through a trusted vendor's update.

options.text: An insider threat
options.rationale: No one inside the victim companies abused legitimate access.

options.text: A DDoS attack
options.rationale: There is no traffic flood.

options.text: A brute-force attack
options.rationale: No passwords were guessed.

questions.explanation: Supply chain attacks deliver compromise through a trusted vendor, software update, or component. Because the update arrives from a trusted third party, it is hard to detect.
questions.discriminator_tested: Supply chain attacks arrive through a trusted third party.

questions.stem: A database administrator who has just resigned is found copying customer records to a personal cloud account, using their legitimate access. What should the response to this insider threat do first?

options.text: Revoke the administrator's access and increase monitoring of related accounts
options.rationale: Correct: removes the access being abused.

options.text: Patch the database software
options.rationale: No software flaw was used; legitimate access was abused.

options.text: Wait for the last working day so the access expires on its own
options.rationale: That leaves the access open while data leaves.

options.text: Reset every customer's password
options.rationale: That does nothing to stop the insider.

questions.explanation: Insider threats come from someone with legitimate access, so the weakness isn't technical. Response includes revoking that access and monitoring.
questions.discriminator_tested: Insider response: revoke access and monitor.

questions.stem: When does incident response planning take place?

options.text: Before incidents occur, preparing plans, teams, tools, and policies in advance
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Only while an incident is in progress
options.rationale: By then it is too late to plan.

options.text: Only after an incident, during the review
options.rationale: The review improves planning, but planning comes first.

options.text: Only when a regulator requests it
options.rationale: Planning is needed regardless of regulators.

questions.explanation: Incident response planning prepares plans, teams, tools, and policies before incidents occur. It is done in advance, not during the incident.
questions.discriminator_tested: Planning happens in advance, not during the incident.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates an incident response plan from an incident response policy?

options.text: The plan is the documented roadmap of roles, procedures, communication, and escalation; the policy sets authority and requirements
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The policy holds the step-by-step procedures; the plan grants authority
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: They are the same document under two names
options.rationale: They serve different purposes.

options.text: The plan is needed only for ransomware
options.rationale: It covers all incident types.

questions.explanation: An incident response plan is a documented roadmap of roles, procedures, communication, and escalation. The incident response policy sets the high-level authority and requirements that the plan operates under.
questions.discriminator_tested: Plan = procedures; policy = authority and requirements.

questions.stem: A company is forming a CSIRT team. Besides security analysts, which two non-technical roles are commonly included? (Choose two.)

options.text: Legal counsel
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Communications or public relations
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A vendor's sales representative
options.rationale: An outside party, not a team member.

options.text: A customer whose data was affected
options.rationale: An outside party, contacted through defined channels.

options.text: A journalist covering the incident
options.rationale: The media are an outside party, handled by the spokesperson.

questions.explanation: A CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) is the group that handles incidents. It is cross-functional and includes non-technical roles such as legal, HR, communications, and management.
questions.discriminator_tested: CSIRTs are cross-functional, including legal, HR, communications, and management.

questions.stem: During an incident, two engineers each changed the same firewall without telling the other, nobody briefed the executives, and an intern gave a reporter a statement. What is the root cause?

options.text: Responsibilities were not specifically defined in advance: no one was assigned to decide, communicate, or act
options.rationale: Correct: every symptom traces back to unassigned roles.

options.text: The firewall was the wrong brand
options.rationale: The problems came from unclear roles, not equipment.

options.text: The intern hadn't had media training
options.rationale: That is a symptom of having no assigned spokesperson.

options.text: The incident was too severe to handle
options.rationale: Severity doesn't explain duplicated effort and gaps.

questions.explanation: Specifically defined responsibilities assign each person's role in advance: who decides, who communicates, and who acts. Clear roles prevent gaps and duplicated effort.
questions.discriminator_tested: Pre-assigned roles prevent gaps and duplicated effort.

questions.stem: Within the incident response plan, what does the business continuity plan cover?

options.text: Keeping critical business functions running during the incident, across the whole business
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Removing malware from infected hosts
options.rationale: That is eradication.

options.text: Deciding when to notify law enforcement
options.rationale: That belongs to outside-party and legal decisions.

options.text: Writing the root-cause report after recovery
options.rationale: That is post-incident activity.

questions.explanation: The business continuity plan keeps critical business functions running during an incident. It is about business-wide continuity, not the technical cleanup of the affected systems.
questions.discriminator_tested: BCP = keep critical business functions running business-wide.

questions.stem: Attackers have taken over the company's email server and may be reading internal messages. The communications plan says incident updates go out by email. What should the communications plan have included?

options.text: Backup communication channels for when the normal ones are compromised
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A rule to send email updates more often
options.rationale: The channel itself is compromised.

options.text: A longer email signature for responders
options.rationale: Irrelevant to the problem.

options.text: No internal updates until the incident is over
options.rationale: Responders still need to coordinate; silence isn't a plan.

questions.explanation: A communications plan defines who is informed, how, when, and by whom, internally and externally. It uses a designated spokesperson, and backup channels matter if normal ones are compromised.
questions.discriminator_tested: Backup channels matter when normal ones are compromised.

questions.stem: After an incident, the team cannot build a reliable timeline: one responder logged times in local time, another in UTC, and a third kept paper notes with no times. What would have prevented this?

options.text: Specifically defined documentation standards, with consistent templates and formats for recording incident details
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A faster SIEM
options.rationale: The problem was how people recorded details, not tool speed.

options.text: More responders
options.rationale: More people would produce more inconsistent notes.

options.text: Shredding the paper notes
options.rationale: That loses information.

questions.explanation: Specifically defined documentation standards set consistent templates and formats for recording incident details. Consistency makes timelines and evidence reliable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Consistent documentation makes timelines and evidence reliable.

questions.stem: What do incident response frameworks such as SANS and NIST give an organization?

options.text: Structured guidance, with a common set of phases and terms for organizing incident response
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A firewall configuration that blocks attacks
options.rationale: Frameworks are guidance, not technical controls.

options.text: A guarantee that no incidents will happen
options.rationale: No framework can promise that.

options.text: A list of every known malware hash
options.rationale: That is threat-intelligence data.

questions.explanation: Incident response frameworks provide structured guidance for organizing incident response. They give a common set of phases and terms, so responders and partners use the same language.
questions.discriminator_tested: Frameworks give common phases and terms.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the six SANS incident response steps in order?

options.text: Preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Identification, preparation, eradication, containment, recovery, lessons learned
options.rationale: Preparation comes first, and containment comes before eradication.

options.text: Preparation, containment, identification, recovery, eradication, lessons learned
options.rationale: Identification comes before containment, and eradication before recovery.

options.text: Preparation, identification, recovery, containment, eradication, lessons learned
options.rationale: Recovery comes after containment and eradication.

questions.explanation: SANS has six steps: preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Unlike NIST, SANS separates containment, eradication, and recovery into their own steps.
questions.discriminator_tested: SANS: six steps, with containment, eradication, and recovery separate.

questions.stem: How does NIST's role in incident response differ from CISA's?

options.text: NIST is a standards body whose publications guide incident response; CISA is an agency that issues alerts and receives incident reports
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: NIST receives incident reports; CISA writes the lifecycle standards
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both are private companies that sell incident response software
options.rationale: Both are US government bodies.

options.text: NIST is a regulator that fines companies after every breach
options.rationale: NIST publishes guidance; it doesn't fine anyone.

questions.explanation: NIST is the US standards body whose publications guide incident response, and it provides the four-phase lifecycle that is commonly tested. CISA is a government agency and reporting point, not a lifecycle model.
questions.discriminator_tested: NIST publishes guidance; CISA is the reporting agency.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 incident response lifecycle phases in order?

options.text: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication, and recovery; post-incident activity
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Detection and analysis; preparation; post-incident activity; containment, eradication, and recovery
options.rationale: Preparation comes first, and post-incident activity comes last.

options.text: Preparation; containment, eradication, and recovery; detection and analysis; post-incident activity
options.rationale: Detection and analysis must come before containment.

options.text: Preparation; identification; containment; eradication; recovery; lessons learned
options.rationale: That is the SANS six-step model.

questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 has four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication, and recovery; and post-incident activity. It combines containment, eradication, and recovery into one phase. Revision 3 (April 2025) supersedes it and aligns to the CSF 2.0 functions.
questions.discriminator_tested: NIST combines containment, eradication, and recovery into one phase.

questions.stem: A small US water utility has detected an intrusion and wants government alerts, guidance, and a place to report the incident. Which organization fits?

options.text: CISA
options.rationale: Correct: the US agency for guidance, alerts, and incident reports.

options.text: SANS
options.rationale: A private training organization whose steps form a framework; it isn't a government reporting point.

options.text: The Diamond Model
options.rationale: An intrusion analysis model, not an organization.

options.text: ISO
options.rationale: An international standards body, not a US reporting point.

questions.explanation: CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, provides guidance, alerts, and a place to report incidents. It is a government agency and reporting point, not a lifecycle model.
questions.discriminator_tested: CISA is a reporting point, not a lifecycle model.

questions.stem: A company trains its response team, buys forensic tools, records normal network baselines, and sets up an on-call contact list. Which incident response phase is this?

options.text: Incident preparation
options.rationale: Correct: all of this is ready before an incident.

options.text: Detection and analysis
options.rationale: Nothing has been detected yet.

options.text: Containment
options.rationale: There is no incident to contain.

options.text: Post-incident activity
options.rationale: No incident has happened yet.

questions.explanation: Incident preparation means having policies, a trained team, tools, baselines, and communication ready before an incident. It is the first phase, and it also covers prevention planning.
questions.discriminator_tested: Preparation is the first phase, done before an incident.

questions.stem: A company has budget to prepare for only a few incident types. How should it decide which to prepare for first?

options.text: Run risk assessments to find the likely threats, vulnerabilities, and most valuable assets, and focus preparation there
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Prepare for whatever was in the news this week
options.rationale: Headlines don't reflect this company's own risks.

options.text: Prepare only for the cheapest scenarios
options.rationale: Cost alone ignores likelihood and impact.

options.text: Skip preparation and handle incidents as they come
options.rationale: Preparation is the first phase for good reason.

questions.explanation: Risk assessments in preparation identify likely threats, vulnerabilities, and valuable assets. They drive priorities, so limited preparation effort goes where it matters most.
questions.discriminator_tested: Risk assessments drive preparation priorities.

questions.stem: An analyst receives an IDS alert, checks logs to confirm it is real, works out which hosts are affected, and rates its severity. Which phase is this?

options.text: Detection and analysis
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Preparation
options.rationale: That happens before any alert.

options.text: Eradication
options.rationale: Nothing has been removed yet.

options.text: Lessons learned
options.rationale: That comes after the incident is resolved.

questions.explanation: Detection and analysis means detecting, validating, scoping, and prioritizing a suspected incident. It follows preparation and determines whether there is an incident and how bad it is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Detection and analysis validates, scopes, and prioritizes.

questions.stem: A responder disconnects an infected laptop from the network and blocks the attacker's IP address at the firewall. Which activity is this, and why?

options.text: Containment, because it limits spread and damage before the cause is removed
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Eradication, because it removes the malware from the laptop
options.rationale: The malware is still on the laptop.

options.text: Recovery, because it returns the laptop to normal service
options.rationale: The laptop is offline, not restored.

options.text: Lessons learned, because it documents the findings
options.rationale: Nothing is being documented here.

questions.explanation: Containment limits spread and damage by isolating hosts, blocking addresses, or disabling accounts. It stops the damage first and comes before eradication.
questions.discriminator_tested: Containment stops damage first; it precedes eradication.

questions.stem: After isolating the affected hosts, the team deletes the malware, removes a backdoor account the attacker created, and patches the exploited flaw. Which phase is this?

options.text: Eradication
options.rationale: Correct: removing the cause.

options.text: Containment
options.rationale: That was the isolation, already done.

options.text: Recovery
options.rationale: Returning systems to service comes next.

options.text: Preparation
options.rationale: That happens before incidents.

questions.explanation: Eradication removes the cause of the incident: malware, compromised accounts, and the exploited weakness. It removes the root cause and follows containment.
questions.discriminator_tested: Eradication removes the root cause, after containment.

questions.stem: A server is rebuilt from a clean image, its data restored from backup, tested, put back into production, and watched closely for signs that the attacker has returned. Which phase is this?

options.text: Recovery
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Eradication
options.rationale: Removing the cause was already done.

options.text: Detection and analysis
options.rationale: Nothing is being detected or scoped.

options.text: Containment
options.rationale: Nothing is being isolated.

questions.explanation: Recovery restores systems to normal operation, verifies them, and monitors for recurrence. It returns systems to service after eradication.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recovery returns to service after eradication, with monitoring.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a post-incident review and lessons learned?

options.text: The review is the meeting that examines what happened; lessons learned are the documented findings that feed back into plans, controls, and training
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The review assigns blame; lessons learned assign punishments
options.rationale: Both aim at improvement, not blame.

options.text: Lessons learned happen before the incident; the review happens during it
options.rationale: Both come after the incident.

options.text: They are identical
options.rationale: One is the meeting, the other its documented output.

questions.explanation: A post-incident review is a meeting after resolution to examine what happened and how it was handled, aimed at improvement rather than blame. Lessons learned are its documented output.
questions.discriminator_tested: Review = meeting; lessons learned = documented output.

questions.stem: Where do lessons learned go after an incident, and why?

options.text: Back into preparation, updating plans, controls, and training so the next incident is handled better
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Into the shredder once the review meeting ends
options.rationale: That throws away their value.

options.text: Only into the prosecution file
options.rationale: That is evidence, not lessons.

options.text: Nowhere; they matter only for the incident just closed
options.rationale: They exist to improve future handling.

questions.explanation: Lessons learned are documented findings that feed back into plans, controls, and training. They are the output that loops back into preparation, closing the lifecycle.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lessons learned loop back into preparation.

questions.stem: Which of these belongs in the incident response policy rather than the incident response plan?

options.text: A statement giving the CSIRT authority to disconnect any system, plus definitions of severity levels
options.rationale: Correct: authority and requirements.

options.text: A step-by-step checklist for isolating an infected laptop
options.rationale: A procedure, so it belongs in the plan.

options.text: A phone tree of on-call contacts
options.rationale: An operational detail of the plan.

options.text: The command syntax for capturing a memory image
options.rationale: A procedure, not policy.

questions.explanation: Creating an incident response policy means setting formal authority, scope, definitions, roles, severity levels, and reporting rules. The policy holds the high-level authority and requirements; the plan holds the procedures.
questions.discriminator_tested: Policy = authority and requirements; plan = procedures.

questions.stem: A journalist calls a junior analyst asking for details of an ongoing breach. The incident response policy documents how information is shared with outside parties. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Refer the journalist to the designated spokesperson without sharing details
options.rationale: Correct: sharing goes through designated people.

options.text: Share the technical details, since the public deserves to know
options.rationale: The analyst isn't authorized to share.

options.text: Deny that any incident is happening
options.rationale: Lying damages trust and may break disclosure rules.

options.text: Post an update on personal social media
options.rationale: That is not an approved channel.

questions.explanation: The policy defines what may be shared with outside parties, with whom, by whom, and through which channels. These decisions are made in advance and routed through designated people, often with legal review.
questions.discriminator_tested: Sharing goes through designated people, decided in advance.

questions.stem: Which two are outside parties that may be involved in an incident? (Choose two.)

options.text: Law enforcement
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The company's ISP
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The CSIRT's incident lead
options.rationale: An internal role.

options.text: The company's own help desk
options.rationale: Internal staff.

options.text: The organization's in-house legal counsel
options.rationale: An internal role, usually on the CSIRT.

questions.explanation: Outside parties are external groups involved in an incident: law enforcement, regulators, ISPs, vendors, customers, and media. Contact them only through the defined channels.
questions.discriminator_tested: Outside parties are external and contacted only through defined channels.

questions.stem: A company suffers a theft of customer data and may want to prosecute. When should it decide how to interface with law enforcement?

options.text: In advance, with legal counsel, so evidence is handled and documented in a way that keeps it admissible
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Only after the systems have been wiped and restored
options.rationale: By then the evidence is gone.

options.text: Never; law enforcement has no role in data theft
options.rationale: Data theft is often a crime law enforcement investigates.

options.text: Whenever any staff member decides to call the police
options.rationale: The decision should be planned and routed, not ad hoc.

questions.explanation: Interfacing with law enforcement means deciding in advance when and how to involve them, with legal counsel. Evidence handling and chain of custody affect whether evidence is admissible.
questions.discriminator_tested: Decide law enforcement involvement in advance; handling affects admissibility.

questions.stem: Why do organizations send reports to incident reporting organizations such as CISA, sector sharing groups, and regulators?

options.text: To meet reporting obligations and share intelligence that helps others defend themselves
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: To transfer legal liability for the incident to the reporting body
options.rationale: Reporting doesn't transfer liability.

options.text: So the reporting organization takes over and runs the response
options.rationale: The organization still runs its own response.

options.text: Because reporting automatically removes the attacker from the network
options.rationale: Reporting doesn't contain or eradicate anything.

questions.explanation: Incident reporting organizations are external bodies that receive incident reports, such as CISA, sector sharing groups, and regulators. Reporting meets obligations and shares intelligence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reporting meets obligations and shares intelligence.

questions.stem: A US federal agency confirms a security incident. Under FISMA requirements, what must it do?

options.text: Report the incident to CISA within the required timeframe
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Decide privately whether reporting is worthwhile
options.rationale: Reporting is mandatory.

options.text: Report it only to its IT contractor
options.rationale: A contractor isn't the reporting authority.

options.text: Wait for the annual audit to mention it
options.rationale: The required timeframes are far shorter.

questions.explanation: FISMA requires US federal agencies to report incidents to CISA within required timeframes. It is a federal reporting obligation, not an optional step.
questions.discriminator_tested: FISMA: federal agencies report to CISA within required timeframes.

questions.stem: Why are ISPs an important outside party during incident response?

options.text: They can filter, trace, or block traffic on their network, upstream of the company
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: They write the company's incident response policy
options.rationale: That is an internal document.

options.text: They pay ransoms on their customers' behalf
options.rationale: ISPs don't do that.

options.text: They automatically remove malware from customer laptops
options.rationale: ISPs act on traffic, not internal hosts.

questions.explanation: ISPs (internet service providers) are an outside party that can filter, trace, or block traffic. They are key for upstream DDoS mitigation, since a flood can fill the link before it reaches the company.
questions.discriminator_tested: ISPs act upstream: filter, trace, or block traffic.

questions.stem: A board member asks whether the company's work on preventing incidents means the CSIRT can be disbanded. What is the best answer?

options.text: No: prevention lowers the number of incidents but cannot eliminate them, so response is still needed
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Yes: patching and hardening stop every incident
options.rationale: No control stops everything.

options.text: Yes: awareness training makes incidents impossible
options.rationale: Training reduces risk; it doesn't remove it.

options.text: No: prevention actually increases the number of incidents
options.rationale: Prevention reduces incidents.

questions.explanation: Preventing incidents means reducing their likelihood through risk assessment, patching, hardening, network and host security, malware defenses, and user awareness. It lowers the number of incidents but cannot eliminate them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Prevention reduces incidents but can't eliminate them.

questions.stem: An employee finds a USB drive in the parking lot and plugs it into a work PC, and malware installs. Which attack vector is this?

options.text: External or removable media
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Attrition
options.rationale: Attrition means brute force.

options.text: Impersonation
options.rationale: No one pretended to be someone else.

options.text: Loss or theft of equipment
options.rationale: Nothing was lost or stolen; a device was brought in.

questions.explanation: Attack vectors are the paths attacks use: external or removable media, attrition (brute force), web, email, impersonation, improper usage, and loss or theft of equipment. A vector is the route of entry, not the attack goal.
questions.discriminator_tested: Attack vector = route of entry.

questions.stem: Web server logs show someone running a vulnerability scanner against the site, but nothing has been exploited yet. Which kind of sign of an incident is this?

options.text: A precursor: a sign an incident may occur in the future
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: An indicator: a sign an incident has occurred or is occurring
options.rationale: Nothing has happened yet.

options.text: An eradication step
options.rationale: Eradication is a response phase, not a sign.

options.text: A lessons-learned finding
options.rationale: That comes after an incident.

questions.explanation: Signs of an incident are precursors (signs an incident may occur in the future) and indicators (signs one has occurred or is occurring). Scanning with no exploitation points to a possible future attack.
questions.discriminator_tested: Precursor = future; indicator = present or past.

questions.stem: Which two are precursor and indicator sources an analyst should use? (Choose two.)

options.text: IDS/IPS, SIEM, and antivirus alerts
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Reports from employees who notice something odd
options.rationale: Correct: people are a source too.

options.text: The antivirus console alone, since one source is enough
options.rationale: No single source is complete.

options.text: The company's marketing calendar
options.rationale: It says nothing about attacks.

options.text: A printed network diagram from five years ago
options.rationale: Out-of-date documentation, not a source of signs.

questions.explanation: Precursor and indicator sources include alerts (IDS/IPS, SIEM, antivirus), logs, publicly available information, and reports from people. There are many sources, and no single one is complete.
questions.discriminator_tested: Many sources; no single one is complete.

questions.stem: Malware is on the company's only order-processing server during peak season, and legal wants evidence preserved for possible prosecution. Which approach best reflects how containment strategies should be chosen?

options.text: Weigh potential damage, evidence needs, service availability, resources, and duration before choosing how to isolate it
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Always power the server off immediately, whatever the cost
options.rationale: That loses volatile evidence and stops orders; it isn't always right.

options.text: Leave it running untouched until peak season ends
options.rationale: That lets the damage continue.

options.text: Wipe and reinstall it at once
options.rationale: That destroys the evidence legal needs.

questions.explanation: Containment strategies are chosen by weighing potential damage, evidence preservation, service availability, time and resources, and duration. The strategy balances stopping the attack against keeping evidence and services.
questions.discriminator_tested: Containment strategy balances stopping damage with evidence and service needs.

questions.stem: An administrator found malware on a server, immediately wiped and reinstalled it, and only then told the CSIRT. Later, legal asks for the evidence. What was missed?

options.text: Evidence gathering and handling: evidence should have been collected and preserved, with each step documented, before wiping
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A faster reinstall
options.rationale: Speed was never the problem.

options.text: Notifying the ISP first
options.rationale: The ISP has no role in a single infected server.

options.text: A larger disk
options.rationale: Irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Evidence gathering and handling means collecting and preserving evidence during response and documenting each step. Gather before wiping, and keep the original intact.
questions.discriminator_tested: Gather evidence before wiping.

questions.stem: During an active attack, an analyst spends hours trying to trace the attacker's source IP address while the attack keeps spreading. What is wrong with this approach to attack sources?

options.text: Identifying the source must not delay containment, and source addresses can be spoofed anyway
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Source IPs are always accurate, so the trace just needed to be faster
options.rationale: They can be spoofed or belong to compromised systems.

options.text: Attack sources should never be investigated
options.rationale: They should be, just not at the expense of containment.

options.text: The analyst should have attacked the source IP in return
options.rationale: Hacking back is illegal and may hit an innocent system.

questions.explanation: Working out attack sources means identifying where the attack came from, such as attacker addresses and related infrastructure. Source addresses can be spoofed, and identifying the source must not delay containment.
questions.discriminator_tested: Source tracing must not delay containment; addresses can be spoofed.

questions.stem: Which order of eradication and recovery activities is correct?

options.text: Remove the malware and disable compromised accounts, fix the exploited weakness, change credentials, restore from clean sources, verify, then return to production
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Restore from backup, return to production, then remove the malware
options.rationale: Restoring before eradication invites reinfection.

options.text: Return to production, verify, and then fix the exploited weakness
options.rationale: The open weakness can be used again right away.

options.text: Change credentials while the malware is still active, restore, and leave the weakness for later
options.rationale: Active malware can capture the new credentials, and the weakness stays open.

questions.explanation: Eradication and recovery activities remove malware, disable compromised accounts, fix the exploited weakness, restore from clean sources, change credentials, and verify. Eradicate the cause before restoring, and verify that systems are clean before returning them to production.
questions.discriminator_tested: Eradicate before restoring; verify before production.

questions.stem: A CSIRT manager wants to hire a second analyst. Which use of collected incident data best supports the request?

options.text: Presenting metrics such as incident counts, time spent per incident, and cost
options.rationale: Correct: data-driven justification.

options.text: Deleting incident records after closure to save storage
options.rationale: That throws away the data needed.

options.text: Describing only the single worst incident
options.rationale: One anecdote isn't data.

options.text: Publishing every incident's raw logs online
options.rationale: That creates a new security and privacy problem.

questions.explanation: Using collected incident data means analyzing incident data and metrics (counts, time spent, cost) to improve controls, plans, and training. It is data-driven improvement, and it also supports resourcing decisions.
questions.discriminator_tested: Incident metrics drive improvement and resourcing.

questions.stem: Under evidence retention, what sets how long incident evidence is kept?

options.text: Policy and legal needs
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Whatever the responder prefers
options.rationale: Retention isn't a personal choice.

options.text: The size of the hard drive alone
options.rationale: Storage space doesn't override legal needs.

options.text: Nothing; evidence is always deleted when the incident closes
options.rationale: Evidence may be needed long after closure.

questions.explanation: Evidence retention means keeping incident evidence for a defined period. The period is set by policy and legal needs rather than by individual choice.
questions.discriminator_tested: Retention period is set by policy and legal needs.

questions.stem: A company is writing evidence retention policies. Which inputs should drive how long and how evidence is kept?

options.text: Legal, regulatory, and organizational requirements
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The preferences of whichever analyst collected the evidence
options.rationale: Policy, not personal preference, decides.

options.text: The storage vendor's marketing claims
options.rationale: Irrelevant to retention needs.

options.text: Only the cost of storage
options.rationale: Cost matters but can't override legal requirements.

questions.explanation: Evidence retention policies are rules for how long and how evidence is kept. They are driven by legal, regulatory, and organizational requirements.
questions.discriminator_tested: Legal, regulatory, and organizational requirements drive retention policies.

questions.stem: Evidence from a breach will likely be used to prosecute the attacker. How does this evidence retention use case affect handling?

options.text: It calls for the most rigorous handling and longer retention, with an unbroken chain of custody
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The evidence can be deleted once the incident report is written
options.rationale: A trial may come much later.

options.text: The use case has no effect on retention
options.rationale: The purpose determines length and rigor.

options.text: Prosecution evidence needs less care than lessons-learned notes
options.rationale: This is reversed.

questions.explanation: Evidence retention use cases include prosecution, internal discipline, audits and regulators, and lessons learned. The purpose determines how long evidence is kept and how rigorously it is handled.
questions.discriminator_tested: Purpose determines retention length and handling rigor.

questions.stem: Which two are evidence retention best practices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Store evidence securely, with access control and integrity checks
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Securely dispose of evidence once its retention period expires
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Keep evidence on a shared drive anyone can browse
options.rationale: Access must be controlled.

options.text: Keep all evidence forever without review
options.rationale: Evidence should be destroyed securely when retention ends.

options.text: Relabel evidence whenever it moves, without recording who moved it
options.rationale: That breaks the chain of custody.

questions.explanation: Evidence retention best practices include secure storage with access control, integrity checks, chain of custody, labeling, and secure disposal when the retention period expires. Protect integrity while evidence is kept, and destroy it securely afterward.
questions.discriminator_tested: Protect integrity while kept; destroy securely afterward.
